label: Non-religious celebration of life
serviceTimelineNote: There is no fixed timetable. Many families hold the celebration two to six weeks after the death, once travel is arranged and there has been a little time to breathe. That extra time is not a delay — it usually makes for a warmer, more personal gathering, and it gives everyone a chance to send photos.

mediaPlacement.guidance: A photo tribute is very much at home here. Most families play it after the first few spoken tributes, when everyone has settled, or right at the end as a gentle close. Five minutes is a comfortable length.
A looping slideshow while guests come in and find seats gives people something kind to look at, and it takes the pressure off the silence. The same photos can play again later without anyone minding.

mediaPlacement.context: At the reception or gathering afterwards
mediaPlacement.guidance: This is where the longer family cut belongs — the one with the extra photos, the in-jokes and the blurry-but-beloved shots. People drift over, point, and start telling stories to each other.

musicGuidance: Anything that sounds like them is right. Favourite songs, the record that was always on, the piece they walked down the aisle to.
If you want a song we cannot include in the video file itself, we can build the video silent and timed to that song, and the venue plays it live. Nothing is lost.
Two or three pieces across the celebration is plenty. Silence between them is not an awkward gap; it is room to feel something.

interviewAdjustments.note: Ask about what they believed in or lived by rather than about religion — kindness, fairness, the outdoors, hard work, a good argument.
Offer a favourite saying, a toast, or a line from a song instead of a prayer.

checklistExtras: Decide who will speak, and roughly in what order.
Check the venue can play a video and has speakers — ask what connection they need.
Choose whether the tribute video plays during the celebration, as people arrive, or both.
deliveryNotes: Bring the video on a USB stick formatted FAT32 or exFAT, and email a copy to whoever is running the sound desk.
Take the printed card for the venue so the person pressing play knows the order and the length.

readings.title: Do Not Stand at My Grave and Weep
readings.source: Attributed to Mary Elizabeth Frye, 1932. She never claimed copyright and the poem circulated anonymously for decades; it is treated as public domain and is read at funerals everywhere.
readings.text:
Do not stand at my grave and weep,
I am not there, I do not sleep.
I am a thousand winds that blow,
I am the diamond glints on snow.
I am the sunlight on ripened grain,
I am the gentle autumn rain.
When you awaken in the morning's hush,
I am the swift uplifting rush
Of quiet birds in circled flight.
I am the soft stars that shine at night.
Do not stand at my grave and cry,
I am not there, I did not die.

readings.title: Crossing the Bar
readings.text:
Sunset and evening star,
And one clear call for me!
And may there be no moaning of the bar,
When I put out to sea,

But such a tide as moving seems asleep,
Too full for sound and foam,
When that which drew from out the boundless deep
Turns again home.

Twilight and evening bell,
And after that the dark!
And may there be no sadness of farewell,
When I embark;

For tho' from out our bourne of Time and Place
The flood may bear me far,
I hope to see my Pilot face to face
When I have crost the bar.

readings.title: Death is Nothing at All
readings.source: Henry Scott Holland, from a sermon preached in 1910 — public domain
readings.text: Death is nothing at all. I have only slipped away to the next room. I am I, and you are you. Whatever we were to each other, that we still are. Call me by my old familiar name, speak to me in the easy way which you always used. Put no difference in your tone, wear no forced air of solemnity or sorrow. Laugh as we always laughed at the little jokes we enjoyed together. Play, smile, think of me, pray for me. Let my name be ever the household word that it always was. Let it be spoken without effect, without the trace of a shadow on it. Life means all that it ever meant. It is the same as it ever was; there is absolutely unbroken continuity. Why should I be out of mind because I am out of sight? I am but waiting for you, for an interval, somewhere very near, just around the corner. All is well.

readings.title: Remember
readings.text:
Remember me when I am gone away,
Gone far away into the silent land;
When you can no more hold me by the hand,
Nor I half turn to go, yet turning stay.
Remember me when no more day by day
You tell me of our future that you plann'd:
Only remember me; you understand
It will be late to counsel then or pray.
Yet if you should forget me for a while
And afterwards remember, do not grieve:
For if the darkness and corruption leave
A vestige of the thoughts that once I had,
Better by far you should forget and smile
Than that you should remember and be sad.
